FUENTE: Historical Archive of the Lesbian-Feminist Movement in Mexico, YMY
ARTICULO: Genesis of the lesbian-feminist and lesbofeminist movements in Mexico, 1970s decade. Ákratas Group 1976

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: HETEROSEXUALITY AS THE FORM OF DOMINATION OVER WOMEN (HETEROPHALLOSEXUALITY)
COMENTARIOS:
HETEROSEXUALITY AS THE FORM OF DOMINATION OVER WOMEN (HETEROPHALLOSEXUALITY). 
Ákratas was very clear that heterosexuality could not be reduced to a simple "sexual relationship between man and woman" as homosexuals claimed to argue that homosexuality was simply the "sexual relationship between two people of the same sex.
No, Ákratas stated that for women, heterosexuality within the patriarchal system could not be any "preference" or "option," but an obligation to exist and to live in society. Heterosexuality was the sexual subordination of women to men and, specifically, the sexual domination of men over women through sexuality. For this reason, she defined it as: heterophallosexuality, because it revolved around the man, the phallus and intercourse, recalling Ann Koedt's book: The Myth of the Vaginal Orgasm. And those women who refused to submit to heterosexuality were brutally punished, repressed and violated, and if they recidivated they were locked up in psychiatric hospitals, prisons or murdered.
FUENTE: Historical Archive of the Lesbian-Feminist Movement in Mexico, YMY
ARTICULO: Genesis of the lesbian-feminist and lesbofeminist movements in Mexico, 1970s decade. Ákratas Group 1976

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: DIVE BARS AND BARS, THE ONLY MEETING PLACE FOR NON-HETEROPHALLOSEXUAL WOMEN

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: THE ONLY POSSIBLE MEETING SPACE FOR NON-HETEROPHALLOSEXUAL WOMEN WERE THE "DIVE BARS"
COMENTARIOS:
THE ONLY POSSIBLE MEETING SPACE FOR NON-HETEROPHALLOSEXUAL WOMEN WERE THE "DIVE BARS".
Despite heterosexist repression, homosexual men could count on many meeting places: bathrooms, streets, canteens, parks, gyms, sports clubs, clubs, cinemas, buses, universities, religious seminaries, exclusively male institutions such as the army, art venues, business trips, artistic activities, among many more and, particularly, the "dive bars". But non-heterophallosexual women were cloistered in the home, attending to children and under the domination and control of a husband; they had no space, their repressive situation was doubly worse than that of homosexuals. 
Except for exceptional cases, it was not until the 1960s that some homosexual women could take refuge on weekends in the "dive bars", covert heterosexual sites that tolerated the presence of all kinds of social eccentricities. Meeting spaces that revolved around the consumption of alcohol and drugs and that admitted the entrance of "social trash", so they were not only clandestine but illegal and, consequently, subjected to continuous repression and violence from the police. In these places gathered: judicial police, traffickers, plainclothes police, male prostitutes, voyeurs, traffickers, coyotes, informants, transsexuals, pimps, sugar daddies, women subjected to prostitution, transvestites, sadomasochists, drug traffickers, queers and faggots and in the midst of all these, dykes, lesbians and manfloras. 
But attendance at dive bars constituted a privilege for those women who managed to become economically independent; most could not access them because it was difficult for them to get a job or steady employment and therefore have money; they depended on their parents or were married and the vast majority had children, besides the fact that it was dangerous to travel late at night without a car.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO:
An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
Background
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: THE FIRST HOMOSEXUAL BARS, CLANDESTINE AND ILLEGAL
COMENTARIOS:
THE FIRST HOMOSEXUAL BARS, CLANDESTINE AND ILLEGAL.
In the 70s, the first "atmosphere" bars emerged, apparently heterosexual spaces but in reality most of the attendees were homosexual. And for that reason, they were constantly raided by the police (razzias) and users were taken in vans to police stations and detained while being extorted with very high fines, threats of being exposed in newspapers (periodicasos) or payment with sex.
For non-heterophallosexual women, they constituted the only way to find similar others, to go out on weekends to breathe a breath of air in the midst of suffocating heterosexual environments, and the rest of the week lead a double life. For this reason, homosexual women of those decades were formed in the midst of alcohol, drugs, sexual excesses and prostitution. And, consequently, in the midst of a high degree of violence, both external, from heterosexuals to homosexuals, and internal, among themselves. 
Precisely, the first struggle that lesbian-feminists initiated was to take non-heterophallosexual women out of the bars, away from alcohol, drugs, prostitution, sexual roles (butch/fem) and violent relationships. All of which does not eliminate the certain "charm" that these places of clandestine, underground, illegal and forbidden life had.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: SPACES, THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN HOMOSEXUALITY AND LESBIANISM: BARS OR PREMISES
COMENTARIOS:
SPACES, THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN HOMOSEXUALITY AND LESBIANISM: BARS OR PREMISES.
Ákratas perfectly understood that "bars" were spaces of human alienation and mental enajenation, therefore it detached itself from any kind of approach to such sites and promoted the feminist initiative of creating healthy spaces to congregate non-heterophallosexual women in order to develop their consciousness and feminist commitment without alcohol, drugs, exacerbated sex, frivolity, banality, or butch/fem sexual roles, galán/lady or compadre/fem and, therefore, without destructive relationships that generated violence among women. 
And in modest apartments of some of its members, the loan of spaces of social struggle, to the rental of premises by cooperation, it was possible to promote the work of small feminist consciousness-raising groups (PGAF) or sexpol groups; theoretical-political discussions and the preparation of public protest actions. 
This was one of the great differences between Lesbian Feminism (FL) and Lesbian-Feminism (LF); FL moved away from female homosexuality that precisely had bars as its meeting point and the whole social context that revolved around them; LF, on the contrary, continued linked to bars and one of its consequences is that it recruited homosexual women who were never interested in feminism and promoted the gayfication of lesbians. And those who did approach did so only to obtain personal benefit from the movement itself, under a totally chauvinistic logic starting to profit from the needs of non-heterophallosexual women. 
In addition, Ákratas focused particularly on community life among women: feminist communes, to offer spaces outside of bars.
FUENTE: Lesbian Reflections No. 1
ARTICULO: SPACES, THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN HOMOSEXUALITY AND LESBIANISM: BARS OR PREMISES

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: ÁKRATAS WORK METHODOLOGY: PGAF, GAF AND RCPF

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: ÁKRATAS WORK WITH FEMINIST METHODOLOGY: (PGAF) SMALL FEMINIST CONSCIOUSNESS-RAISING GROUP
COMENTARIOS:
ÁKRATAS WORK WITH FEMINIST METHODOLOGY: (PGAF) SMALL FEMINIST CONSCIOUSNESS-RAISING GROUP.
ÁKRATAS Group continued working with the feminist methodology of Small Feminist Consciousness-Raising Groups (PGAF), sexpol groups, which gave rise to the feminist movement itself. But toward its complete development, that is, to the second level, the Feminist Action Groups (GAF) and to the third level, the Feminist Political Coordination Networks (RCPF). Many women's groups started the first level but did not pass to the following ones, limiting themselves to group psychotherapy that at an individual level allowed them to be functional within the patriarchal system, without confronting this system -as would happen with the next group Lesbos-. 
Some groups moved to the second level, GAF, of public affirmative actions, some of which made history, but did not develop a structure of organic articulation with other groups and lacked a future projection. 
And precisely, when such articulation between different organizations was beginning to be created and a future political projection designed, they were halted by the Rubinist anti-feminist counter-revolution (Gayle Rubin) in the next decade of the 80s in the US and Mexico, thus managing to stop and dismantle the powerful nascent feminist movements: both the radical (FR) and the socialist feminist (FS).
FUENTE: OFF OUR BACKS
ARTICULO: Akratas -- lesbian/feminism in mexico

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: PARTICIPATION OF ÁKRATAS IN AN EVENT ORGANIZED BY THE COALITION OF FEMINIST WOMEN (CMF)
COMENTARIOS:
PARTICIPATION OF ÁKRATAS IN AN EVENT ORGANIZED BY THE COALITION OF FEMINIST WOMEN (CMF).
Ákratas decided not to join the Coalition of Feminist Women (CMF, 1976), nor did the heterosexual feminist group La Revuelta, as both were located in the line of radical feminism (FR) opposed to the liberal feminism (FL) that prevailed in the Coalition. But Ákratas, furthermore, assumed a lesbian feminist position (FL) and defined itself specifically as separatist -both from liberal and heterophallocentered feminism (of the Coalition), and from mixed organizations of men and women (heterosexuals with whom La Revuelta did maintain a relationship) and, of course, detached from homosexuals for being men and therefore beneficiaries of the patriarchy. 
However, Ákratas came to participate in some events organized by the CMF that it considered politically important, such as a meeting held in mid-April to publicize the Coalition's objectives to new interested parties, held at Los Talleres de arte in Coyoacán, precisely when the famous photograph of Marcela Olavarrieta with her arms raised showing one of the most important symbols of the feminist movement was taken, subsequently published in the magazine Bandera Socialista No. 79 of September 1978.
FUENTE:
Bandera Socialista
No. 79, Sept 15, 1978
ARTICULO: Bandera Socialista

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: THE LESBIANS' STRUGGLE FOR THEIR DEMANDS WITHIN THE FEMINIST MOVEMENT, THE CMF (1976)

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: PARTICIPATION OF THE INITIATOR OF THE FIRST LESBIAN GROUP IN MEXICO IN THE GROUP: MEXICAN FEMINIST MOVEMENT
COMENTARIOS:
PARTICIPATION OF THE INITIATOR OF THE FIRST LESBIAN GROUP IN MEXICO IN THE GROUP: MEXICAN FEMINIST MOVEMENT.
Article by Marta Lamas where she points out that, at the beginning of 1976, the MLM (Women's Liberation Movement) conducted an evaluation and decided to open up to more members. A new group arrived at its premises called: Mexican Feminist Movement (MFM) with Lourdes Arizpe, Mireya Toto and Yan María Castro (Yaoyólotl). 
Of these three, Mireya along with Esperanza Brito and Anilú Elías of the National Women's Movement (MNM) sponsored the formation of the first alliance of feminist groups in Mexico, the Coalition of Feminist Women (CMF) in October 1976. And Yan María would be the first feminist promoter of the lesbian-feminist perspective within the Mexican feminist movement. It should be clarified that Marcela Olavarrieta was the initiator of lesbian feminism (FL) or feminism first in 1976, but Yan María of lesbian-feminism (LF) or lesbianism first in 1977 (which decades later she would consider a historical error not to have followed the line that Ákratas proposed).
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: My first ten years: MAS and MLM.

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: FAILED ATTEMPT TO INCLUDE THE DEMAND: "AGAINST THE REPRESSION OF NON-HETEROSEXUAL WOMEN", IN THE MFM AGENDA
COMENTARIOS:
FAILED ATTEMPT TO INCLUDE THE DEMAND: "AGAINST THE REPRESSION OF NON-HETEROSEXUAL WOMEN", IN THE MFM AGENDA.
Article by Sonia Riquer, member of the Women's Collective (CM) of the PRT (Revolutionary Workers' Party, Trotskyist), in which she mentions that upon joining the Collective to the Coalition, Mireya (Toto) and Jean (Yan) "... who at those times still shared the Mexican Feminist Movement (MFM) group" were in it. This fact refers to Yan detaching herself from the MFM because it did not accept including the urgent demand of lesbians: to fight against the brutal repression of which women who refused to submit to forced heterosexuality were victims.
After her exit from the MFM, Yan focused on searching within the Coalition for those interested in promoting the inclusion of said fourth demand as part of the three axes of struggle of the Coalition: 1- for abortion; 2- against rape and 3- against violence against women; and the fourth axis would be: 4- "against the repression of women who refused to submit to heterosexuality". 
Facing the fear of Coalition activists regarding the topic of lesbianism, she found only one interested party, Cristina Val. The few homosexuals who were close to the Coalition rejected being identified as "lesbians" and, furthermore, saw it as completely absurd and ridiculous to propose "organizing as lesbians". It should be mentioned that these same individuals would become the most aggressive enemies against lesbians themselves, starting the war of homosexual-gay women within feminism itself against lesbian women.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: Twenty years of feminist presence in Mexico.

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: PHOTOGRAPH OF THE PROMOTER OF THE STRUGGLE AGAINST REPRESSION OF LESBIANS IN A PROTEST ORGANIZED BY THE CMF

PHOTOGRAPH OF THE PROMOTER OF THE STRUGGLE AGAINST REPRESSION OF LESBIANS IN A PROTEST ORGANIZED BY THE CMF.

Participation of the initiator of the lesbian-feminist movement in Mexico, Yan María Castro Yaoyólotl, as a member of the CMF, with a sign of the Women's Collective (CM), in June 1978.
Photograph by Ana Victoria Jiménez.

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: BASES OF DEPARTURE OF THE LESBOS GROUP
COMENTARIOS:
BASES OF DEPARTURE OF THE LESBOS GROUP.
This article is useful because it exposes the political characterization of the first two lesbian-feminist groups in Mexico: Lesbos 1977 and OIKABETH 1978, which allows understanding the bases of departure of the former:
1- Lesbos and Oikabeth emerged within the feminist movement, not within the homosexual movement. And they constituted the beginning of the lesbian current of Mexican feminism (having as precedent its matrix in Ákratas);
2- both defended the principle of political autonomy (PAP), that is: self-organization, self-management and self-direction of women, without the control of the political leadership of men and
3- Lesbos started from a moderate separatism, it did not establish any type of link with men; Oikabeth started from autonomism, establishing links only with homosexual and heterosexual men of the left, never with those of the right, maintaining its political autonomy.
FUENTE:
FEM Magazine, No. 163. 
20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH. Introduction
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: PHOTOGRAPHS OF THE INITIATORS OF THE FIRST LESBIAN FEMINIST GROUP IN MEXICO, LESBOS GROUP 1977
COMENTARIOS:
PHOTOGRAPHS OF THE INITIATORS OF THE FIRST LESBIAN FEMINIST GROUP IN MEXICO, LESBOS GROUP 1977.
Photographs of the first nine members and founders of Lesbos Group in the second week of August 1977; lacking the precise day, August 13 was estimated as an average. Founders: Yan María Castro (Yaoyólotl); Cristina Val.; Lety La Lenta; Amira La Armenia, María Elena La Buena; Lety La Güera; La Pichi Cartié; La 6:20 and Lupe El Raro. 
Photographs of most are not presented out of respect for their current privacy or because it still implies risks for them, but the names with which we knew them are preserved (some discriminatory denominations were later worked on to overcome them); we do not know the real names of several to date. Nonetheless, their place in history as founders of the first lesbian feminist group in Mexico is preserved. 
Also participated: Diana P., Gonzáles Gonzáles, Tina La Machina, R. Rodríguez, La rapidita, Divina Garza, Alicia S., La No Hay Problema, Las glorias de Gloria, Luisa, Cuidado y Te Juntes, Laurita La Chiquita, La del 302, King Kong, Silvita Volcán, Sálvese Quien Pueda, La Vecina de Cristina, Alice Wolker, La Víctima, La Hay Te Voy, Quien No Cuida Pierde, Doble Sánchez, La Micrófono, Pa´qué te Arrimas (si no te animas), La Dentista, La Monumentoza, La ¡Huau¡, Adrianita, La Oculta, El Zarpazo, Laurita 2, Sin Dolor No Hay Amor, Gabriela, Yola La Exquisita and La Discreta, among others more, who encouraged the public demonstrations with or without hood, and whose names will remain printed with gold letters in the book of history. 
The two initiators of the group, given their feminist training, suggested that the group be called "Lesbos" but the newly integrated homosexual women found it high-sounding and very aggressive but accepted it provisionally; the following year, after a heated discussion, it would be reaffirmed. 
Domicile of foundation of Lesbos: Cristina Val.'s house, Gabriel Mancera #1164, apt. 4, Col del Valle, Mexico City.
FUENTE: AHMLFM-YMY
ARTICULO: Portraits of Lesbos members

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: WHY YAN YES AND NANCY NO
COMENTARIOS:
WHY YAN YES AND NANCY NO. 
Following the line of argument of the lecture: Why Marcela yes and Nancy no, presented at the Homosexual Movement in Mexico Forum at UAM-X in April 2001, indisputably Nancy was the most prominent promoter of the gay homosexual movement in Mexico, but Marcela and Yan of the lesbian feminist movement in Mexico. Because, as already noted, Nancy opposed the existence of a lesbian movement; she considered it inadmissible for it to be independent of the homosexual movement and called lesbians divisive and fragmenters of lesbian-gay unity for being exclusionary and elitist. Yan, unlike Nancy, always defended the political autonomy of the lesbian movement, its independence from homosexuals (although for many, she made the mistake of establishing alliances later with left-wing homosexuals, the FHAR). 
For Nancy, the central point was the homosexual struggle, for Yan, the struggle of lesbians; Nancy sought gay liberation, Yan seeked women's emancipation; Nancy fought against heterosexism, Yan against patriarchy. More specifically, Nancy sought gay liberation within the patriarchy and Yan sought the emancipation of women by abolishing said patriarchy. To which is added that Nancy was a liberal gay with leftist progressive ideas and Yan a Marxist socialist feminist.
Lecture published in 2001 referring to 1976.
FUENTE: AHMLFM-YMY
ARTICULO: Why Yan yes and Nancy no.

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: HISTORICAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A FEMINIST WORKING MEETING WITH PARTICIPATION OF ÁKRATAS AND LESBOS
COMENTARIOS:
HISTORICAL PHOTOGRAPH OF A FEMINIST WORKING MEETING WITH PARTICIPATION OF ÁKRATAS AND LESBOS. 
This photograph has great historical significance because for the only time the two founders of Lesbos and the main founder of Ákratas appear together, taking into account that in those times lesbians avoided being photographed so as not to be identified due to repression.
Marcela Olavarrieta of Ákratas (bottom left); Yan María Castro Yaoyólotl and Cristina Val. of Lesbos (top right); Lilia Mayer (bottom right) and the feminist movement photographer Ana Victoria Jiménez (center), among other comrades. 
Photograph from Ana Victoria Jiménez's camera, 1979.
FUENTE: Photographic camera of Ana Victoria Jiménez
ARTICULO: Photograph with the Founder of Ákratas Group, Marcela Olavarrieta and the founders of Lesbos Group, Cristina V. and Yan María C.

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: THE STRUGGLE FOR THE INCLUSION OF LESBIAN DEMANDS

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: ABSENCE IN THE FEMINIST PROGRAM OF THE STRUGGLE AGAINST REPRESSION OF NON-HETEROSEXUAL WOMEN
COMENTARIOS:
ABSENCE IN THE FEMINIST PROGRAM OF THE STRUGGLE AGAINST REPRESSION OF NON-HETEROSEXUAL WOMEN. 
Yan María and Cristina considered that feminist demands were absolutely important and urgent but were heterophallocentered, that is, focused on heterophallosexuality: 1- for abortion, 2- against sexual rape and 3- against violence from the husband to the wife, the three centered on the subjection of women by men and, for that reason, did not include the savage repression exerted against non-heterophallosexual women (that is, not submitted to a man), totally invisibilizing the reality of lesbians. 
Both considered it very unfair that lesbians were always supporting the struggle of heterophallocentered feminists, but that the latter did not support the struggle of lesbian feminists. Therefore, it was necessary to propose the famous "fourth demand" or fourth axis: 4- "against the repression of non-heterosexual women," in order to be integrated into the three demands or three axes of struggle of the Coalition. 
Note: The date mentioned in the article: "August 77" is in an incorrect place since it corresponds to the foundation of the group, and this fragment refers to May when its formation process began.
1996 magazine referring to 1977.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: PROPOSAL TO THE CMF FOR THE INCLUSION OF A "FOURTH DEMAND": AGAINST THE REPRESSION OF NON-HETEROSEXUAL WOMEN
COMENTARIOS:
PROPOSAL TO THE CMF FOR THE INCLUSION OF A "FOURTH DEMAND": AGAINST THE REPRESSION OF NON-HETEROSEXUAL WOMEN.
Both lesbians, in a timid and discrete manner, dared to personally propose to some of the Coalition's leaders the need for the feminist movement to include a fourth demand: 4- "Against the repression of non-heterosexual women," since there was terrible violence against this sector of women. But those leaders argued that the assumption of lesbianism was a risk for the nascent feminist movement in Mexico, that if Mexican society had difficulty accepting feminism, it would tolerate the reclamation of lesbianism even less. 
Those heterophallocentered feminists did not yet understand the revolutionary feminist character of lesbianism; they reduced it to "sex between women," that is, to "female homosexuality," which was precisely what they were trying to avoid and, furthermore, they did not understand that lesbianism was the most radical expression of women's struggle and, therefore, their political rebellion.
1996 magazine referring to 1977.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: ARGUMENTS OF HETEROPHALLOCENTERED FEMINISTS FOR NOT INCLUDING THE FOURTH LESBIAN DEMAND
COMENTARIOS:
ARGUMENTS OF HETEROPHALLOCENTERED FEMINISTS FOR NOT INCLUDING THE FOURTH LESBIAN DEMAND.
The arguments of heterophallocentered feminists for not including lesbians' petition within the feminist program, the famous "4th demand," were similar to those held by men of the left for not taking feminism into account: that feminism divided the unity of the working class and the left; that when socialism was established women would obtain their freedom; that women should not organize separately, autonomously, but fight along with men; that particular and individualistic struggles should not be established; that the struggle of women should not be addressed as a matter separate from the class struggle, etc.
And since then, in Mexico, feminist leaders belonging to the liberal feminism (FL) current never accepted lesbianism until today in 2018; they always tried to avoid its presence or leave it marginal and therefore invisibilized. That liberal feminism (FL) would be precisely the one that would transmute into: genderism (gender theory, TG).
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: AFTER SAID REFUSAL, DECISION TO FORM A LESBIAN GROUP WITHIN FEMINISM
COMENTARIOS:
AFTER SAID REFUSAL, DECISION TO FORM A LESBIAN GROUP WITHIN FEMINISM.
Initially, the two lesbians never thought of constituting a lesbian group, as they thought that feminism itself should include the struggle of women who refused to submit to forced heterosexuality because they were women. Theoretically, feminism should represent the interests of all women, but in practice it was heterophallocentered, that is, it did not submit heterosexuality to questioning as part of patriarchal control of men over women. 
Therefore, after the Coalition's refusal, they decided it was necessary to form a group specifically of lesbians within feminism itself to demand the struggle against forced heterophallosexuality. But they did not foresee that it would be the beginning of the separation between "non-heterocentered women" and "heterocentered women" which would lead to the misunderstood division: "feminists" (heterosexuals) and "lesbians" (homosexuals), as if all feminism were heterosexual and lesbianism were female homosexuality.
And said marginalization would lead to: 1) lesbians moving away from feminism because they felt marginalized by it and closer to homosexual groups to protect themselves from savage heterosexist repression, which led to lesbianism becoming homosexualized and abandoning feminism and 2) feminists increasingly focusing on a heterophallocentered vision of the world, moving away from the critical and radical lesbian-feminist vision, and moving closer to a patriarchal vision that would lead to genderism (gender theory (TG)). 
On one hand, lesbians lost feminism by becoming homosexualized, and on the other, heterocentered feminists became patriarchalized by transforming into genderists, a situation that would not have been possible with a lesbian-feminist vision of feminism.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: IMPOSSIBILITY OF FINDING OTHER LESBIANS IN FEMINISM, THE LEFT AND SOCIAL MOVEMENTS
COMENTARIOS:
IMPOSSIBILITY OF FINDING OTHER LESBIANS IN FEMINISM, THE LEFT AND SOCIAL MOVEMENTS.
The two lesbians faced the fact of not finding more lesbians interested in forming a group within the Coalition itself. Feminist comrades simply panicked with such a proposal, and the few homosexuals infiltrated in feminism rejected and repudiated the very proposal of lesbianism as a political position (later, as already mentioned, these same individuals would become fearsome enemies of lesbians themselves within feminism, the Rubinists (Gayle Rubin).
With much more reason, it was impossible to find lesbians among the members of social movements, left-wing parties, unions, socialist organizations and revolutionary movements, for whom such a proposal was completely crazy, reactionary and counter-revolutionary. In this regard, it should not be forgotten that at that time neither the right, nor the left, nor capitalists, nor socialists considered anything related to the topic of sexuality, or women; therefore, one could not categorically demand that the left understand lesbianism.
This explains why the group would be formed by women of the middle class or petty bourgeoisie who were not politicized and even had conservative and right-wing tendencies, who later would oppose the first revolutionary proposals of the left-wing and socialist lesbians, their leader starting in 1980 being Patria Jiménez, the first gay congresswoman in Latin America in 1997.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: Castro, Yan María and M, Luz María

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: ARRIVAL AT BARS IN SEARCH OF THOSE INTERESTED IN FORMING A LESBIAN GROUP

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: SEARCHING FOR LESBIANS OUTSIDE THE FEMINIST MOVEMENT AND THE SOCIAL LEFT: BARS
COMENTARIOS:
SEARCHING FOR LESBIANS OUTSIDE THE FEMINIST MOVEMENT AND THE SOCIAL LEFT: BARS.
Finding no interest in forming a lesbian group among feminists, social struggles and the left, the two lesbians set out to find interested parties in the only sites where homosexual women gathered, that is, bars. 
Bars were a kind of oasis in the midst of the desolate heterosexist social desert that, despite being mired in alcohol, drugs, compulsive sex and violent relationships, constituted the refuge and only meeting place among women who did not wish to submit to forced heterosexuality. For women they were very important because -unlike homosexuals- they did not have the multiple spaces to be able to find each other even if they were clandestine: bathrooms, streets, cinemas, parks, canteens, back of buses, gyms, sports clubs, clubs, religious seminaries, corporations, the army, business trips, etc. etc.
It should be noted that at that time, even lesbians themselves still confused "lesbianism" with "female homosexuality" as if they were the same, because they did not yet have much clarity about the antagonism between both (an error that would later bring very negative consequences against the lesbian groups themselves).
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: DIFFICULTIES FOR THE FORMATION OF THE GROUP
COMENTARIOS:
DIFFICULTIES FOR THE FORMATION OF THE GROUP.
The formation of the group was extremely difficult as it constituted a deeply repressed social sector: at an external level, persecuted and punished by all social institutions: family, neighborhood, school, profession, culture, religion, etc. and, at an internal level, by the psychic interiorization of all that repression manifested in guilt, self-rejection, self-punishment and violence against oneself and, therefore, expressed in aggression and repudiation toward others who were their similar mirrors, the strong violence that presented among homosexual women.
Many homosexuals approached the group because word spread in bars that a group was being formed and many thought it was a party group or to find girlfriends, which was very important for them because no other option existed to contact similar women. Most attended to flee the terrible repression they suffered; to use it as a personal therapeutic group; to cover the deep loneliness they experienced; to find a girlfriend, disappear and return later for another; to look for "fresh meat" the machinas or butchs; to party with others, etc., a situation that constantly upset the development of the group and made it difficult to articulate a lesbian feminist organization. 
At first few came to value this completely new space without alcohol, drugs, butch/fem roles, or destructive relationships typical of the gay environment. Over the years some came to highly value these spaces and particularly the lesbian feminists who made them possible.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: FOUNDATION OF LESBOS GROUP ON AUGUST 13, 1977
COMENTARIOS:
FOUNDATION OF LESBOS GROUP ON AUGUST 13, 1977. 
Photographs of the first nine members and founders of Lesbos Group in the second week of August 1977; lacking the precise day, August 13 was estimated as an average. Founders: Yan María Castro (Yaoyólotl); Cristina Val.; Lety La Lenta; Amira La Armenia, María Elena La Buena; Lety La Güera; La Pichi Cartié; La 6:20 and Lupe El Raro. 
Photographs of most are not presented out of respect for their current privacy or because it still implies risks for them, but the names with which we knew them are preserved (some discriminatory denominations were later worked on to overcome them); we do not know the real names of several to date. Nonetheless, their place in history as founders of the first lesbian feminist group in Mexico is preserved. 
Also participated: Diana P., Gonzáles Gonzáles, Tina La Machina, R. Rodríguez, La rapidita, Divina Garza, Alicia S., La No Hay Problema, Las glorias de Gloria, Luisa, Cuidado y Te Juntes, Laurita La Chiquita, La del 302, King Kong, Silvita Volcán, Sálvese Quien Pueda, La Vecina de Cristina, Alice Wolker, La Víctima, La Hay Te Voy, Quien No Cuida Pierde, Doble Sánchez, La Micrófono, Pa´qué te Arrimas (si no te animas), La Dentista, La Monumentoza, La ¡Huau¡, Adrianita, La Oculta, El Zarpazo, Laurita 2, Sin Dolor No Hay Amor, Gabriela, Yola La Exquisita and La Discreta, among others more, who encouraged the public demonstrations with or without hood, and whose names will remain printed with gold letters in the book of history. 
The two initiators of the group, given their feminist training, suggested that the group be called "Lesbos" but the newly integrated homosexual women found it high-sounding and very aggressive but accepted it provisionally; the following year, after a heated discussion, it would be reaffirmed. 
Domicile of foundation of Lesbos: Cristina Val.'s house, Gabriel Mancera #1164, apt. 4, Col del Valle, Mexico City.
FUENTE: AHMLFM-YMY
ARTICULO: Portraits of Lesbos members

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: PHOTOGRAPH OF A LESBOS GROUP MEETING AT THE END OF A PGAF WORK SESSION
COMENTARIOS:
PHOTOGRAPH OF A LESBOS GROUP MEETING AT THE END OF A PGAF WORK SESSION. 
This photograph corresponds to the year 1978 but offers an idea of the original group that started in 1977, a few months earlier, in that same place; furthermore, it is the only one available. Most participants are facing away for fear of public exposure due to repression, which explains why it was not customary to take photographs of the group. 
Surprisingly, despite the historically relevant role played by these initiators of the first group, most are currently not publicly visible, making it impossible to count on their personal testimonies.
Photograph from 1978, photographer unknown.

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: PARTICIPATION OF LESBOS GROUP IN THE COALITION OF FEMINIST WOMEN (CMF)

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: PARTICIPATION OF LESBOS GROUP IN THE COALITION OF FEMINIST WOMEN (CMF)
COMENTARIOS:
PARTICIPATION OF LESBOS GROUP IN THE COALITION OF FEMINIST WOMEN (CMF). 
This article by Marta Lamas mentions that: "In 1977 the Coalition's premises are a hub of meetings and projects. The Women's Collective and Lesbos, the first group of organized lesbians, join". 
It should be clarified that only a part of Lesbos joined the CMF; most of the new members did not want to participate because heterocentrism or heterophallocentrism prevailed in the Coalition by the leading feminists and therefore, the marginalization of lesbians. 
The lack of political experience of the new members did not allow them to understand that a slow and deep work of consciousness-raising had to be carried out to overcome millennia of rejection and persecution against those women who did not submit to forced heterophallosexuality and that, therefore, one could not demand from heterosexual feminists an immediate and unquestioned acceptance of lesbianism. But, above all, they did not understand that it was not "lesbianphobia of all feminists," but of the right-wing part of feminists, the HFALF, that is, the "liberal feminists" or anti-lesbianfeminist heterofeminists; who a decade later would be in charge of halting and dismantling feminism itself under the discourse of gender, genderism, and therefore, for whose purposes, lesbian feminism represented their greatest obstacle. 
1996 magazine referring to 1977.
FUENTE:
FEM Magazine, No. 163. 
20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: My first 10 years: MAS and MLM

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: ÁKRATAS AND WOMEN'S COMMUNES
COMENTARIOS:
ÁKRATAS AND WOMEN'S COMMUNES.
Ákratas was not interested in joining the feminist movement, the CMF, due to its liberal and heterophallocentered character, for which it was not interested in supporting Lesbos's effort. Ákratas thought that attention should not be focused on joining existing initiatives as they were permeated by patriarchy, that new forms of women's struggle, new organizational structures and new ways of doing politics from feminism should be created.
For this reason, Ákratas focused on supporting the efforts that various women's groups from several countries, mainly the US and Western Europe, had initiated since the second half of the 1960s toward the creation of communes; but not from a patriarchal starting point like the hippie communities where "sexually liberated" women continued to serve men or communities that maintained passive and apolitical lifestyles largely based on addictions. 
Ákratas visualized a new international social system based on women's communes not only to defend themselves from the abuses and violence of men, but so that they could develop integrally and in fullness; otherwise they could never do so. The family was the cellular unit of patriarchy, the commune was the cellular unit of feminism.

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: NOMADIC OR RADICAL TRAVELING WOMEN AND SEPARATISTS IN MEXICO
COMENTARIOS:
NOMADIC OR RADICAL TRAVELING WOMEN AND SEPARATISTS IN MEXICO.
Toward the end of the 60s and during the 70s a great movement of nomadic or traveling women took place, moving from imperial-colonialist countries to third world ones, and to a lesser extent from the latter to the former. Women who, moreover, in their majority, were radical and separatist, at least in those times. Ákratas maintained important contact with these women, so several of them were part of the group although intermittently during their travel periods. 
But for Lesbos it was the first contact of organized Mexican lesbianism with radical and separatist lesbianism (except for co-founder Yan María who promoted said contact because she herself had been a nomad). As mentioned, most members of Lesbos were from the conservative middle class but contact with nomads influenced the understanding that the only way women could develop was by maintaining their total independence, that is, separate, from men. For this reason Lesbos never intended to approach or unite with homosexuals, maintaining a kind of non-explicit moderate separatism.
1996 magazine referring to events of 1977.
FUENTE:
FEM Magazine, No. 163. 
20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: FIRST PARTICIPATION IN MEXICO OF LESBIANS WITH THE LEFT, HUNGER STRIKE OF THE COMMITTEE FOR THE PERSECUTED, DISAPPEARED AND POLITICAL EXILES.

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: FIRST PARTICIPATION IN MEXICO OF LESBIANS WITH THE LEFT, HUNGER STRIKE OF THE COMMITTEE FOR POLITICAL PRISONERS
COMENTARIOS:
FIRST PARTICIPATION IN MEXICO OF LESBIANS WITH THE LEFT, HUNGER STRIKE OF THE COMMITTEE FOR POLITICAL PRISONERS.
First incursion of two members of the first organized group of lesbian feminists in an act of the Mexican left, the hunger strike organized by the NATIONAL COMMITTEE PRO-DEFENSE OF PRISONERS, PERSECUTED, DISAPPEARED AND POLITICAL EXILES (CPDPDEP) on August 28, 1977 in the atrium of the Metropolitan Cathedral of Mexico City. The strike aimed to demand the presentation of more than 400 disappeared people in the country held in clandestine prisons, military camps or murdered. A surprising situation for the families of those affected, who without understanding why two deviants or lesbians were present at that event were respectful of their support.
Said participation was the initiative of two members of Lesbos, Yan María and María Elena, at an individual level but as lesbians, not as a group because it was not yet politicized. The important thing about this action is that it represented the beginning of the public presence of lesbian feminists in political events of social struggles and the Mexican left.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine No. 7
ARTICULO: The National Committee Pro-Defense of Prisoners, Persecuted, Disappeared and Political Exiles.

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: LESBIAN SUPPORT FOR THE URUGUAYAN CONFERENCES IN EXILE AGAINST DICTATORSHIP AND IMPERIALISM
COMENTARIOS:
LESBIAN SUPPORT FOR THE URUGUAYAN CONFERENCES IN EXILE AGAINST DICTATORSHIP AND IMPERIALISM. 
Attendance of two members of Lesbos, Yan María and La 620, as lesbians in support of The Uruguayan Culture Conferences in Exile held from August 21 to 28, 1977 in place.
In 1973 the Uruguayan people were subjected to a military dictatorship with a civilian appearance behind which was the US through the CIA, which would last twelve years. Freedom of thought, press, parties and unions were prohibited and imprisonment (seven thousand prisoners) and murder of opponents, particularly of the Tupamaro National Liberation Movement guerrilla, were imposed. As a call for international solidarity, these conferences were organized in Mexico to show the resistance of the people in exile. The conferences gathered artists from several countries: Tania Libertad, Daniel Viglietti, Camerata Punta del Este, Silvio, Pablo Milanés and Teatro El Galpón. The latter an artistic expression that the founder of the first homosexual group in Mexico, FHAR, would question the following year for comparing the military to homosexuals, leaving FHAR aside the essence of the conferences, the struggle against imperialism and dictatorship. This would be the first news of a left-wing homosexual group for Lesbos members.
FUENTE: Third World Notebooks No. 16
ARTICULO: Uruguayan culture conferences in exile. August 21 and 28, 1977

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: PARTICIPATION OF LESBOS GROUP IN THE SECOND NATIONAL CONFERENCE FOR ABORTION
COMENTARIOS:
PARTICIPATION OF LESBOS GROUP IN THE SECOND NATIONAL CONFERENCE FOR ABORTION. 
In September, the Coalition of Feminist Women (CMF) organized the Second National Conference on Abortion where Lesbos Group participated with much shyness and discretion so as not to discomfort heterosexual feminists.
In the article, the incorporation into the Coalition of two more groups, the Women's Collective and La Revuelta, is mentioned as an important achievement; the latter never adhered fully because it considered that the main promoting group of the Coalition, MNM, was close to the dictatorial party in power, the PRI. And care was taken not to mention the incorporation of Lesbos Group which had just integrated a month before.
From then on, in the following public presentations and in CMF publications, the growth of the same was proudly mentioned with "six groups" where the five (four) from before and the two new ones, the Collective and La Revuelta, appeared, completely disappearing the Lesbos group.
These actions were very painful for lesbians. But at that time they did not yet understand that the rejection was not on the part of "feminism," but of the dominant current "liberal, right-wing, pro-capitalist feminism" (which a decade later would become "genderism").
FUENTE:
FEM Magazine, No. 163.
20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: On modest naives and fierce fighters

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: FIRST ARTICLE IN MEXICO WRITTEN BY THE FIRST LESBIAN FEMINIST GROUP FOR THE MAGAZINE, FEM

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: FIRST ARTICLE IN MEXICO WRITTEN BY THE FIRST LESBIAN FEMINIST GROUP FOR THE FIRST FEMINIST MAGAZINE, FEM
COMENTARIOS:
FIRST ARTICLE IN MEXICO WRITTEN BY THE FIRST LESBIAN FEMINIST GROUP FOR THE FIRST FEMINIST MAGAZINE, FEM.
Thanks to two (closeted) contacts that the two initiators of Lesbos Group had on the editorial board of FEM magazine, they learned that in the upcoming issue "5" of October-December of that year 1977, articles from the feminist groups that integrated the Coalition were going to be published, for which, they "notified the group" to present an article. Fortunately said "contacts" made it possible for Lesbos Group to remain in the history of Mexican feminism as one of the five member groups of the first Coalition of Feminist Women (despite the fact that in reality it never formally assumed it) and therefore, to appear both as a member of the Mexican feminist movement (and not the homosexual one) and as the first specifically lesbian-feminist group in Mexico in the 70s decade (Ákratas, 1976, was feminist and lesbian, not specifically lesbian).
Summarized content of the Lesbos Group article: Lesbian movement: political organization; along with the struggle of marginal sectors; against repressive socioeconomic systems capitalism and socialism (Stalinist); for the construction of a new social organization. The system reproduces among the social sectors themselves, but becomes a danger for it when these unite among themselves; lesbians do not fulfill the function for which women were programmed: motherhood and domestic work that sustain the patriarchal system, whose basis is the family, and it is the questioning of heterosexuality and monogamy as transmission of private property and man's control over woman. 
It should be highlighted in this article is a questioning not only of heterosexism -as homosexual or gay women did- but, above all, of the economic and political system, as well as its emphasis on the construction of a new society -and not adaptation to the existing one-. And likewise, a questioning of the family, heterosexuality and monogamy as means of control over women -in opposition to the purposes of homosexual and gay women to achieve conforming families and gay marriage-.
FUENTE: Lesbos
ARTICULO: Lesbian movement

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: FIRST PUBLIC EMERGENCE OF A LESBIAN MEMBER OF THE FIRST LESBIAN FEMINIST GROUP IN MEXICO, FIRST MEXICAN-CENTRAL AMERICAN SYMPOSIUM ON RESEARCH ON WOMEN

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: FIRST TIME IN MEXICO, A MEMBER OF THE FIRST LESBIAN GROUP CAME OUT PUBLICLY AS LESBIAN
COMENTARIOS:
FIRST TIME IN MEXICO, A MEMBER OF THE FIRST LESBIAN GROUP CAME OUT PUBLICLY AS LESBIAN.
For the first time in Mexico, a woman came out publicly as a lesbian as a member of the first group of organized lesbians in the history of the country, Lesbos Group. This fact represented the beginning of the emergence into the public spotlight of the lesbian-feminist movement in the nation. 
This event took place at the First Mexican-Central American Symposium on Research on Women held from November 7 to 9, 1977, at the CIESS (Center for Social Research and Studies). 
In this regard it is important to clarify that certainly Nancy Cárdenas was the first person in Mexico who manifested publicly in defense of homosexuals, but not of lesbianism, nor as a lesbian, not even when in 1975 being opposed to lesbianism she signed the "Declaration of Mexican Lesbians" prepared by foreign lesbian-feminists. Nancy always opposed the construction of a lesbian identity and the formation of a lesbian movement, accusing it of being divisive and splitting the unity of homosexual men and women. For this reason, she was never recognized by lesbians as their initiator but as an opponent, which explains why the lesbian movement in Mexico from the 1980s decade distanced itself from Nancy, although it was respectful of her.
It should be clarified that for the first time in Mexico it was Yan María Castro Yaoyólotl who came forward publicly as a lesbian, but she used the pseudonym: Jeanne Beltrán, not out of fear of public aggression because she was already a public social fighter, but out of fear of the rejection she would suffer from the revolutionary left organizations with which she worked, which considered homosexuality and lesbianism a degeneration of capitalism; her fear lay in that they could consider her an infiltrator of the right and imperialist interests. But the Symposium opened a unique opportunity to take the subject of lesbianism out of invisibility and silence and place it for the first time in public affairs, and in the midst of fears she decided to come forward publicly.
FUENTE:
FEM Magazine, No. 163. 
20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: C., Yan María and M., Luz María

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: FIRST PRESENTATION IN MEXICO ON THE SUBJECT OF LESBIANISM FROM LESBIANS THEMSELVES IN A PUBLIC EVENT
COMENTARIOS:
FIRST PRESENTATION IN MEXICO ON THE SUBJECT OF LESBIANISM FROM LESBIANS THEMSELVES IN A PUBLIC EVENT.
First public presentation in Mexico of a conference on the subject of lesbianism from lesbians, this being a satanized taboo and a subject exclusive to psychiatry and criminal law and whose name was simply unpronounceable. 
Panel 5. Family, Sexuality and Reproduction. Coordinator: Marta Lamas. Paper: Lesbianism and its meaning, by Jeanne Beltrán from UNAM. Proceedings of the First Mexican-Central American Symposium on research on Women, of the Colegio de México.
The concept of "lesbianism" was so aggressive and frightening that the organizers initially changed it to "homosexuality" but the author managed to position the concept of lesbianism; however, the complexity of the subject caused the title to undergo several changes. 
Certainly, in 1975 the concept of "lesbians" was heard for the first time in Mexico in a statement drafted by foreign lesbian-feminists at the IWY who looked for a Mexican woman, Nancy Cárdenas, to sign it; but it remained as that, an initiative of foreigners and passed into oblivion, it was not given continuity because it was not an initiative nor a political position of Mexican women. The Mexican lesbian feminist groups that began to emerge from 1976 on had no type of link with said initiative of the IWY foreigners.
The Proceedings are located in the COLMEX library with entry number 021-1977.
FUENTE: Proceedings of the First Mexican-Central American Symposium on research on Women Nov 7-9, 1977. CIESS (Center for Social Research and Studies).
ARTICULO: The First Mexican-Central American Symposium on Research on Women. Lesbianism and its meaning

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: FIRST QUESTIONING IN MEXICO BY LESBIANS OF HETEROSEXUALITY AS PART OF THE PATRIARCHAL CAPITALIST SYSTEM
COMENTARIOS:
FIRST QUESTIONING IN MEXICO BY LESBIANS OF HETEROSEXUALITY AS PART OF THE PATRIARCHAL CAPITALIST SYSTEM.
For the first time in Mexico lesbian feminists publicly questioned heterosexuality as part of the capitalist system and from a socialist feminist perspective: Jeanne Beltrán. 
For the first time in Mexico, lesbians dared publicly to question heterosexuality, a surprising proposal in the country because it was an untouchable, unquestionable and sacred subject due to the Catholic religion; the subject was even worse because heterosexuality was considered an instrument of the capitalist system to control women and it was clarified that lesbianism was not reduced to "sex between women" but was a political position against the patriarchy, proposals that broke with all parameters established up to that point. Although the paper had argumentative deficiencies and still mixed lesbianism with homosexuality in several aspects, it marked the beginning of the process of political positioning of lesbians in Mexico. 
Main points proposed in the paper: "... the political position of organized political lesbians (Beltrán), carrying out the questioning of heterosexual monogamy and highlighting the utility it provides to the system," Proceedings of the First Mexican-Central American Symposium on research on Women.
FUENTE:
Proceedings of the First Mexican-Central American Symposium on 
Research on Women Nov 7-9, 1977. COLMEX
ARTICULO: The First Mexican-Central American Symposium on Research on Women. Summary of the papers

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: FIRST ARTICLE IN A MEXICAN NEWSPAPER ON THE SUBJECT OF LESBIANISM EXPLAINED BY A MEMBER OF THE LESBIAN MOVEMENT

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: FIRST ARTICLE IN MEXICO BY A NATIONAL CIRCULATION NEWSPAPER ON LESBIAN PARTICIPATION IN A PUBLIC EVENT
COMENTARIOS:
FIRST ARTICLE IN MEXICO BY A NATIONAL CIRCULATION NEWSPAPER ON LESBIAN PARTICIPATION IN A PUBLIC EVENT.
First interview in Mexico by a national circulation newspaper, Unomasuno, which dared to touch on the subject of lesbian feminist participation in a public event without treating it as a mental or physical pathology. For the first time in Mexico the Unomásuno newspaper dared to publish an article on the forbidden subject of lesbianism: "Lesbianism, a challenge to the system, says writer Jeanne Beltrán," written by journalist Patricia Cardona about the presentation of the paper at the First Mexican-Central American Symposium. 
Summary of the content: Capitalism tolerates lesbianism as long as it remains hidden, minoritarian, dispersed and repudiated by society; heterosexuality is the basis of the family institution because it guarantees the production of children, the labor force for capital; marriage is the direct control of a man over a woman and monogamy the transmission of private property. Capital makes survival difficult for those who do not live in marriage and in family like single women and lesbians. Lesbianism is the attempt to break with the direct oppression exerted by capital over women through men.
It should be noted that Beltrán still confused lesbianism with homosexuality because she still had a Foucaultian (Foucault) influence that entered into contradiction with her feminism and her Marxism.
FUENTE: UNOMÁSUNO Daily
ARTICULO: Lesbianism, a challenge to the system, says writer Jeanne Beltrán

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: BEGINNING OF THE CO-OPTATION OF THE FEMINIST MOVEMENT IN THE U.S. STARTING FROM THE INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR
COMENTARIOS:
BEGINNING OF THE CO-OPTATION OF THE FEMINIST MOVEMENT IN THE U.S. STARTING FROM THE INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S YEAR.
In the International Women's Year (IWY) the US government committed to funding with five million dollars the holding of a national meeting of women, the National Women's Conference in the United States which was held in November 1977 in Houston, Texas, with 12 thousand observers and 2 thousand delegates, resulting in 26 resolutions, two of the most important being in relation to abortion and lesbianism. 
This event meant for radical and socialist feminists the co-optation of the women's struggle through government funding (buying of consciences) of the women's movement, as well as the co-optation of lesbianism itself, stripping them of their radical political content. This event represented the beginning of the process of formal integration of liberal feminism (FL) into the patriarchy to form the neo-patriarchy.
Since then, feminism began to orient itself toward genderism (gender theory, TG) (Gayle Rubin) forming a feminist right that began to gain great strength driven by government and private financial support.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 5
ARTICULO: National Women's Conference in the United States.

PLECAS_TITULOS_6: FIRST PUBLIC EXPRESSION OF A LESBIAN GROUP AS PART OF THE CMF, FEM MAGAZINE

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: APPEARANCE OF THE FIRST LESBIAN FEMINIST GROUP IN MEXICO AS PART OF THE CMF, LESBOS GROUP
COMENTARIOS:
APPEARANCE OF THE FIRST LESBIAN FEMINIST GROUP IN MEXICO AS PART OF THE CMF, LESBOS GROUP. 
Despite the fact that Lesbos Group was never formally integrated by the Coalition of Feminist Women (CMF), it managed to appear in FEM magazine as one of the five member groups of the same in issue 5 of October-December 1977. 
This fact was transcendental for the development of lesbianism in Mexico by placing it within the feminist movement and not within the homosexual movement and, therefore, also outside gayness, glbticity and sexual diversity.
These two articles constituted the basis on which the feminist origin of the lesbian movement in Mexico in 1977 was based, facing the systematic denial or disparagement of its existence by gay and sexual diversity historiography.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.

COMENTARIOS:
FEM MAGAZINE ARTICLE: PIECES OF A JIGSAW PUZZLE, LESBOS AS PART OF THE FIVE GROUPS THAT COMPOSED THE CMF.

FEM specified that it did not intend to unify the diverse positions within Mexican feminism, but to unify forces around a common goal respecting the autonomy of each organization.

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: OMISSION OF LESBOS GROUP IN THE OCTOBER 2, 1977 MARCH IN TLATELOLCO
COMENTARIOS:
OMISSION OF LESBOS GROUP IN THE OCTOBER 2, 1977 MARCH IN TLATELOLCO. 
Photograph and note from FEM magazine about the participation of "the six member groups of the Coalition of Feminist Women (CMF)" in the October 2, 1977 demonstration. In which mention is made of: Women's Liberation Movement, Women's Collective, Mexican Feminist Movement (which never managed to consolidate), Lucha Feminista Group (which joined after Lesbos), National Women's Movement (which was not from the left, but from the right) and Lesbos Group was deliberately omitted and in its place the La Revuelta Collective was included which by being radical actually did not belong to the CMF. 
Fact that annoyed the new Lesbos members even more, distancing them from feminism; without understanding that the rejection came from Liberal Feminism (FL) which had to be fought and not from Radical Feminism (FR) with which alliances had to be established. This lack of understanding led many homosexual women to become enemies of feminism and erroneously identify: feminism=heterosexuality, an identification that persists to this day presenting feminism as an affair of heterosexuals that has nothing to do with women who do not submit to compulsory heterophallosexuality.
1978 document alluding to 1977.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine No. 7
ARTICULO: Photograph and note: Feminists and the October 2 demonstration

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: BOOK THE NEW WAVE OF FEMINISM IN MEXICO BY ANA LAU JAIVEN, OMISSION OF LESBOS
COMENTARIOS:
BOOK THE NEW WAVE OF FEMINISM IN MEXICO BY ANA LAU JAIVEN, OMISSION OF LESBOS.
Despite the historical evidence, historians specialized in feminism in Mexico such as Ana Lau Jaiven, an admirer of Marta Lamas, have systematically omitted the important participation of lesbian feminist groups in the movement, and not for lack of documentary information but for heterosexist and lesbianphobic discrimination and for the reductionism of feminism to heterophallocentered matters, that is, not questioning heterophallosexuality as one of the mechanisms of control of men over women. Pages 18 and 19.
But even more, the invisibilization of lesbian feminism has been a postmodern neoliberal political tactic to hide the most radical part of the feminist movement and to this the neoliberal genderist theorists have contributed, because by making lesbianism disappear, the political praxis that can undermine the bases to sink the patriarchal system disappears and said theorists are beneficiaries of this system for which they do not intend to destroy it but to safeguard it.
FUENTE: Planeta Edit.
ARTICULO: The new wave of feminism in Mexico

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: THE NEW WAVE OF FEMINISM IN MEXICO BY ANA LAU JAIVEN, REDUCTION OF LESBOS TO "SMALL GROUP OF HOMOSEXUAL WOMEN"
COMENTARIOS:
THE NEW WAVE OF FEMINISM IN MEXICO BY ANA LAU JAIVEN, REDUCTION OF LESBOS TO "SMALL GROUP OF HOMOSEXUAL WOMEN". 
Ana Lau Jaiven was forced to mention Lesbos Group pressured by the two articles from FEM No. 5, but she made that forced mention as: "small group of homosexual women," page 217, an offensive denomination against lesbians when they have systematically insisted on not being called "homosexual women" but "lesbian women" and not only that, but also "lesbian feminists". 
And the "small group" part was to disparage the lesbian group when it quantitatively managed to gather up to thirty women in its consciousness-raising groups and up to around two hundred in the marches. Furthermore, qualitatively, lesbians were the most participative and boldest part in feminist events without making it explicit; the fact that heterofeminists had the formal representation and discursive handling did not invalidate the important silent participation of lesbians. 
Likewise, Marta Lamas, in the articles on the history of feminism in Mexico published in Debate Feminista, refused to include the experience of the participation of members of the lesbian feminist groups in the Mexican feminist movement of the 70s and 80s decades leaving them out of the history of feminism in total invisibility. And to fill said void, she included gay and queer women infiltrated in feminism to talk about lesbianism knowing they were not lesbians but gay and queer, and even knowing they were enemies of lesbian-feminists themselves. But this is not accidental; Marta Lamas represents within feminism the HFaLF political stance (anti-lesbofeminist heterofeminism) that has as one of its objectives eliminating from the history of Mexican feminism the most rebellious expressions of the same because she is part of the neo-patriarchal system.
FUENTE: Planeta Edit.
ARTICULO: The new wave of feminism in Mexico

TITULO_COMENTARIOS: CONTACT WITH A NEW INTERESTED PARTY IN WORKING IN THE GROUP, LUZ MARÍA MEDINA
COMENTARIOS:
CONTACT WITH A NEW INTERESTED PARTY IN WORKING IN THE GROUP, LUZ MARÍA MEDINA.
At the beginning of December of this year 1977, after surviving a police attack on a gay bar from which several people managed to flee, Cristina Val. met Luz María Medina whom she invited to meet the Lesbos Group that met at her house. But because the group was concluding its last session due to Christmas dynamics, Luzma integrated formally by January of the following year 1978.
Luz María arrived in January with an organizational design for the group, taking advantage of her specialty in administrative medicine, for which she would be considered an "honorary co-founder" because she gave it more structure, a new process that would be called: the restructuring of the group. 
It should be clarified that the difference between Yan and Cristina and Luz María is that the first two came directly from feminism and always maintained their activism in it. Luz María did not; she identified as homosexual and came from the "gay scene," but was very interested in the struggle for lesbian emancipation, for which she stood out from the others.
FUENTE: FEM Magazine, No. 163. 20th Anniv. Our History
ARTICULO: An experience within the lesbian groups of Mexico, 70s, autonomous line, Lesbos and OIKABETH.
AUTORAS: Castro, Yan María and M, Luz María
